A RADIUS server entry with ISE's address and shared secret
Right. The switch needs to know where to send requests and how to protect them.
A static route to the supplicant's subnet on the core switch
Routing to the client plays no role.
A VTY line access class that limits who can log in
This limits management logins to the switch.
An AAA method list for dot1x that uses the RADIUS group
Right. The method list tells the switch to use RADIUS for 802.1X logins.

q.q: Posture passes and ISE wants the session to be re-evaluated so the switch applies the new full-access result. What does ISE send to the switch?
o: An Access-Challenge to the endpoint
This message is part of the original authentication.
A syslog message to the switch
Syslog does not change a session.
A CoA request with a reauthenticate action
Right. The switch restarts authentication for the session and gets the new result.
A DHCP renew request
DHCP is not used to change authorization.

q.q: ISE sends a CoA, but the switch never acts on it. Which switch configuration is missing?
o: ip radius source-interface with the switch's loopback address
A source interface sets the address used in requests and does not accept CoA.
aaa server radius dynamic-author with ISE as a client
Right. The switch must be set up to accept dynamic authorization from ISE.
ntp server for ISE
Time synchronization is not the cause.
A larger MAC address table
Table size does not affect CoA.

q.q: A device moved to a new VLAN by CoA still has its old IP address, and it cannot renew it. Which CoA action fixes this for a device that does not react to the VLAN change?
o: Port bounce
Right. Dropping the link for a moment makes the device ask for a new address on the new VLAN.
Reauthenticate
Reauthentication changes the result but does not make the device renew its address.
Session query
This only asks for session details.
Disconnect without a bounce
Disconnect ends the session and does not force the device to renew its address.

q.q: A host sends thousands of DNS NULL and TXT queries a day for names such as a81c90f3d2e2.telemetry-svc.example, each with a different long string. What is the most likely activity?
o: A DNS amplification denial of service
Amplification uses forged requests to flood a victim with large replies.
DNS cache poisoning
Poisoning plants false answers in a resolver's cache.
A normal software update check
Updates use stable names, not a fresh random string each time.
Data exfiltration through DNS tunneling
Right. Data is packed into the long subdomain names, and the attacker's name server reads the queries.

q.q: Which control best limits employees copying files to a personal cloud storage account over HTTPS?
o: Blocking TCP port 21 at the edge firewall
Port 21 is FTP, and the upload uses HTTPS.
Inline DLP with tenant controls
Right. These can tell a personal account from the unit's own tenant and block sensitive uploads.
Shortening the DHCP lease time on the lab VLAN
Lease time does not affect uploads.
Requiring longer user passwords for every account
A password rule does not stop a signed-in user from uploading.

q.q: An alert fires. The playbook automatically looks up the IP in threat intelligence, opens a ticket and isolates the endpoint, with no analyst typing. Which category of tool does this?
o: SIEM
A SIEM collects and correlates events and raises the alert.
A vulnerability scanner
Scanners look for weaknesses and do not respond to alerts.
SOAR
Right. SOAR runs automated playbooks that connect tools and take response actions.
NetFlow collector
A flow collector records traffic and does not run response steps.

q.q: Which description matches a SIEM correlation rule?
o: It combines events from several sources into one alert
Right. Combining sources is what lets a SIEM see an attack no single log shows.
It encrypts logs as they are collected and stored at rest
Encryption is a storage and transport matter.
It blocks traffic at the switch port when a rule matches
A SIEM detects and alerts. It does not enforce at the port.
It normalizes fields from one source into a data model
Normalizing fields supports searching, but correlation joins events across sources.

q.q: What is the main difference between Cisco XDR and a basic log-collecting SIEM?
o: XDR works only on endpoints and servers, not other tools
XDR spans endpoint, network, email, cloud and other sources.
XDR correlates across tools and ranks incidents
Right. It turns telemetry from many products into ranked incidents with actions an analyst can take.
XDR needs no data from other products to build incidents
It depends on telemetry from integrated products.
XDR is a replacement for a firewall at the network edge
XDR is a detection and response platform and does not filter traffic.

q.q: Which TWO statements about SIEM and SOAR are correct? (Choose two.)
o: A SIEM gathers logs from many systems and correlates them to find threats
Right. This is the core job of a SIEM.
A SIEM replaces the need for any log sources once it is installed
A SIEM depends on data from log sources.
A SOAR tool collects raw packets from every switch on the network
Packet collection is a sensor function.
A SOAR playbook can enrich an alert and open a ticket
Right. Playbooks automate repeated steps so analysts work faster.
A SIEM runs response playbooks natively without SOAR
Automated playbook response is what SOAR adds. A SIEM's core job is to collect and correlate.

q.q: A unit wants Duo to allow access to an app only from managed devices. Which approach fits?
o: Duo Push alone sent to the user's phone
Push verifies the user's approval and not whether the device is managed.
A longer remembered-device period of 30 days
This lowers how often users are asked and does nothing for device trust.
Allowing every IP address in the unit's own range
Location alone does not prove the device is managed.
A device trust policy for managed devices
Right. Duo can require proof that the device is managed before access is allowed.

q.q: Attackers keep sending push requests hoping a tired user will approve one. Which Duo feature best defends against this?
o: Verified Push with a typed code
Right. The user must confirm the code from the login they started, so an unknown push is ignored.
A longer push timeout for slow responders
This gives attackers more time.
Remembering devices for 90 days at a time
This reduces prompts and does not help here.
SMS passcodes only, sent to the registered phone
Text codes can be phished and do not stop push abuse.

q.q: What does this Splunk search return?
o: The five source IP addresses with the most blocked events
Right. It counts blocked events per source IP, sorts from the largest and keeps the first five.
The five source IPs with the fewest blocked events
The sort uses a minus sign, so the largest counts come first.
All blocked events deleted from the firewall index
Searches read data. They do not delete it.
Only the total number of blocked events
The count is split by source IP, not totaled.
q.code: index=firewall action=blocked | stats count by src_ip | sort -count | head 5

q.q: In Splunk Enterprise Security 8.x, what does a detection (formerly a correlation search) create for analysts to triage?
o: A lookup table
A lookup holds reference data and does not create work items.
A data model
Data models organize fields for fast searching.
A summary index
A summary index stores saved search results.
A finding in the analyst queue
Right. Before ES 8.0 a finding was called a notable event. Findings appear in the analyst queue (formerly Incident Review) for analysts to work.

q.q: One IP address triggers the same Splunk alert 500 times in ten minutes and floods the SOAR queue. What is the best fix?
o: Delete the correlation search that raised the alert
This removes detection entirely.
Raise the index retention
Retention does not change alerting.
Turn off the SOAR integration
This hides the symptom and loses automation.
Throttle the alert by source IP for a set time
Right. Throttling suppresses repeats for the same value during the period.

q.title: Find why a lab VPN tunnel will not come up
q.scenario: The unit's lab has two practice firewalls. The tunnel from FTD-LAB1 to the branch peer 198.51.100.2 will not come up. You are authorized to run read-only show and debug commands on FTD-LAB1 only. Work out why the tunnel is down. Do not change or clear any configuration.
q.ticket: TCK-7710: lab site-to-site VPN down. Authorized for read-only checks on FTD-LAB1. Report the cause in the ticket.
q.intro: FTD-LAB1 diagnostic CLI (lab). Type a command.

cmds.out:
Type escape sequence to abort.
Sending 5, 100-byte ICMP Echos to 198.51.100.2, timeout is 2 seconds:
!!!!!
Success rate is 100 percent (5/5), round-trip min/avg/max = 1/1/2 ms

crypto ikev2 policy 10
 encryption aes-256
 integrity sha256
 group 14
 prf sha256
 lifetime seconds 86400
crypto ikev2 enable outside

crypto map OUTSIDE_MAP 10 match address VPN-TRAFFIC
crypto map OUTSIDE_MAP 10 set peer 198.51.100.2
crypto map OUTSIDE_MAP 10 set ikev2 ipsec-proposal AES256
crypto map OUTSIDE_MAP interface outside

IKEv2-PROTO-2: (14): Received Packet [From 198.51.100.2:500/To 192.0.2.1:500]
IKEv2-PROTO-2: (14): Exchange type: IKE_SA_INIT, flags: INITIATOR
IKEv2-PROTO-1: (14): Failed to find a matching policy
IKEv2-PROTO-1: (14): Received policies: encr AES-CBC-256 integ SHA256 prf SHA256 DH group 19
IKEv2-PROTO-1: (14): Sending no proposal chosen notify
All possible debugging has been turned off
[lab] That erases the crypto settings of the whole firewall, including tunnels that work. Stop and tell your lead. A check must not break anything.

checks.t: Confirmed that no IKEv2 security association exists
checks.why: An empty IKEv2 table shows that the first phase never completed, so the problem is early in the negotiation and not in the traffic rules.

checks.t: Pinged the peer to rule out a routing or reachability problem
checks.why: The peer answers, so the path is fine. The failure is in the negotiation and not in the network path.
It shows the local side offers Diffie-Hellman group 14. You need this to compare with what the peer sends.

checks.t: Watched an IKE attempt with the debug
checks.why: The peer proposes DH group 19 and the local policy allows only group 14, so the result is no proposal chosen. The two sides must share one proposal.

checks.t: Did not erase any crypto configuration
checks.why: Clearing the crypto configuration would break working tunnels and was not asked. Diagnosis should leave the setup as it is.

q.title: Find the data theft hiding in DNS logs
q.scenario: The unit's lab uses a cloud DNS security service. An analyst exports a short sample of DNS activity from lab computers. Mark every line that belongs to the suspicious activity, then say what the log shows.
q.ticket: Alert 5521: unusual DNS volume from one lab PC. Read the log only. No changes are asked.

lines.text: 09:14:01 LAB-PC-07 A    update.vendor.example            Allowed  Software Updates
lines.why: A normal software update lookup with a stable name and a known category.
A TXT query with a long random-looking label to a domain nobody has categorized. This is how data can be packed into a DNS name.

lines.text: 09:14:04 LAB-PC-12 A    intranet.unit.example            Allowed  Business Services
lines.why: An ordinary lookup of the unit's own intranet site.
The same PC and the same parent domain, with a new random label two seconds later. Repeating with new strings is the pattern of a tunnel.
A normal lookup of a reference website.
A third query with a fresh random label to the same domain. Nothing a person browsing would produce.
The policy blocked a gambling site. That is the service doing its job and is not part of this alert.
The fourth in a row. The length, the TXT type and the steady rhythm all point to data leaving through DNS.
A normal lookup of a webmail site over IPv6.

ask.label: What does this log show?
opts: One PC sending data out through DNS tunneling to an uncategorized domain
A flood of forged DNS replies aimed at the lab
Users visiting sites the policy should have blocked
ask.why: One PC keeps asking TXT questions with a new long random label under one unrated domain. The labels carry data out, and the attacker's name server reads them. Block the domain and review the PC.

q.title: Roll out 802.1X in the lab without locking people out
q.scenario: The unit's lab will move its access switch ports to 802.1X with ISE. Some devices, such as printers, cannot run a supplicant. Build the rollout in a safe order, starting with a few pilot ports. Some ideas do not belong. Add the steps in the order they should happen.
q.ticket: CHG-3382: lab 802.1X pilot. Approved window Saturday 0800 to 1200. Pilot ports only.

rules.text: Add the switch to ISE as a network device with a shared secret
rules.why: ISE answers only devices it knows. Without this entry the switch's requests are dropped.

rules.text: Set up RADIUS, AAA and dot1x system-auth-control on the switch
rules.why: The switch must send 802.1X and MAB requests to ISE before anything can be checked.

rules.text: Enable open mode with dot1x and MAB on the pilot ports
rules.why: Open mode lets traffic flow while authentication is tried, so people keep working and ISE gets to see every device.

rules.text: Review the ISE live logs for devices that fail or have no supplicant
rules.why: The logs show which printers, phones and other devices need an entry or a policy before enforcement.

rules.text: Add authorization policies and MAB entries for the devices you found
rules.why: Each legitimate device gets the access it needs, so it will still work when the port stops allowing unauthenticated traffic.

rules.text: Switch the pilot ports from open mode to enforcing mode
rules.why: Only now are policies ready, so closing the port will not lock out the devices that belong.

rules.text: Enforce closed mode on every access port on the first day
rules.why: Without a pilot and logs, devices that cannot run a supplicant would lose access at once.

rules.text: Turn off ISE logging to reduce noise during the pilot
rules.why: The logs are how you find the devices that need policies. Turning them off removes the information you need.

before.why: The logs only show devices once open mode has made them try to authenticate.
You write policies for devices you found in the logs, not for a guess.

last.why: Enforcing comes last because it blocks unauthenticated devices. Doing it earlier risks locking out legitimate ones.

q.title: Place the parts of a zero trust path to a private app
q.scenario: A contractor with a managed laptop needs to reach one internal application in the unit's lab data center. Nothing may be opened inbound on the data center firewall, and the contractor must not get access to the rest of the network. Place each part in its spot. Three parts in the tray do not belong in this design.
q.ticket: CHG-4410: contractor access to one lab application. Authorized by the lab owner. No inbound firewall openings.

slots.label: Spot A
slots.hint: a trust decision made before any session starts

slots.label: Spot B
slots.hint: the policy broker in the cloud

slots.label: Spot C
slots.hint: the inside-out link to the cloud

devs.name: Duo MFA
devs.why: Duo checks the user with a second factor and can check device health, so identity is proven before access is brokered.

devs.name: Secure Access ZTNA
devs.why: The cloud service applies the policy and connects the user to the one approved private application, not to the network.

devs.name: Resource connector
devs.why: The connector sits in the data center and builds an outbound tunnel to the cloud, so no inbound firewall opening is needed.

devs.name: Secure Firewall (east-west rules)
devs.why: Internal firewall rules allow the app only the servers it needs, so a compromise cannot spread freely.

devs.name: ISE wired access policy
devs.why: ISE controls access for devices that connect to the unit's own switches and wireless. It is not part of this remote path.

devs.name: Secure Email Gateway
devs.why: This product filters email. It has no role in reaching a private application.

devs.name: Wireless LAN controller
devs.why: A controller manages the unit's access points and has no role in reaching an app from the internet.

q.title: Find why 802.1X never starts on a lab switch port
q.scenario: A lab laptop on switch SW-LAB2 port Gi1/0/12 never starts 802.1X, though ISE is reachable and the port is set for 802.1X. You are authorized by the lab owner to change SW-LAB2 only. Find the missing piece and fix it with one global command. Do not turn off AAA.
q.ticket: TCK-7733: SW-LAB2 Gi1/0/12 no 802.1X. Authorized to change SW-LAB2 in the lab. Do not touch other switches.
q.intro: SW-LAB2 (IOS XE, lab). Lab shortcut: global configuration commands work without typing configure terminal.

aaa new-model
aaa authentication dot1x default group radius
aaa authorization network default group radius
aaa session-id common
 dot1x pae authenticator

Sysauthcontrol              Disabled
Dot1x Protocol Version      3

Dot1x Info for GigabitEthernet1/0/12
-----------------------------------
PAE                       = AUTHENTICATOR
QuietPeriod               = 60
ServerTimeout             = 0
TxPeriod                  = 30

Auth.      Acct.      Both
Maximum inQ length:    NA        NA          1
Number of packets sent:        0          0          0
Number of packets received:    0          0          0
[lab] That turns off all AAA, including admin logins to this switch. Stop and tell your lead.

checks.t: Read the AAA and dot1x lines in the running configuration
checks.why: The AAA and port lines are present, so the missing piece is not there. The global 802.1X switch is not in the list.
